chunks: "RISC machines keep the instruction set small and regular: fixed-length instructions, only loads and stores touch memory, and arithmetic works on a big register file.
CISC instructions are richer, variable length, and can do things like add a value straight from memory. The advantages of RISC are mostly in hardware.
Fixed-length, uniform instructions make decoding trivial, so the decoder is small and you can decode several per cycle.
Every instruction goes through roughly the same stages, which makes pipelining clean and keeps the clock fast and the CPI close to one.
The control logic is smaller and uses less area and power, and it leaves room for more registers or cache. It's also easier for compilers to generate good code for a regular ISA.
CISC's argument is code density and fewer instructions, which was a big deal when memory was expensive.
In terms of the Iron Law, CISC lowers instruction count but tends to raise CPI, and RISC does the reverse. In practice today the line has blurred.
Modern x86 cores split CISC instructions into RISC-like micro-ops internally, so you pay for that decode in area and power at the front end.
That's partly why Arm and RISC-V do well in power-limited devices."
